issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: For a 35-year-old single male special education teacher reporting a mugging/robbery, 'I have failed in my most important role in life' is hard to link coherently to the rest of the profile. The other appraisals center on self-blame and persistent danger, but this item implies a salient role failure theme (e.g. partner/parent/protector) that is not otherwise represented in triggers, threat, or memory.

issues.item: Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
issues.explanation: Within Memory, intense shame and intense rage on recall can coexist, but paired with a mugging/robbery and the rest of this profile they pull toward different meanings of the event without enough support elsewhere. Shame would usually connect to strong self-blame/humiliation themes, while rage would connect to injustice/anger themes; the profile does not integrate both clearly.

vignette:
Daniel, a 35-year-old European American special education teacher who had never married and lived alone in a small apartment near the school where he worked, described the robbery as the moment his sense of ordinary safety was split into “before and after.” One evening, while walking home after staying late to prepare materials for the next day’s classes, he was approached on a quiet street by two men who shouted at him to stop. The force of their voices, abrupt and aggressive, made the encounter feel instantly out of his control. One of the men grabbed him roughly, and in the struggle Daniel twisted awkwardly and injured his neck, an ache that lingered in the days afterward and became hard for him to ignore whenever he felt tense. The men took his belongings quickly and left him shaken and humiliated, and when police arrived afterward he found their presence unsettling in a different way: the uniforms, the questions, and the attention from authority made the whole event feel strangely sharpened, as though he were still standing there under interrogation rather than already back on the sidewalk.

In the weeks that followed, Daniel found that the memory came back to him in a vivid, almost mechanically exact way. He said that remembering the robbery was “like looking at photographs,” with separate images that seemed fixed and unreal at the same time: the men’s faces, the streetlight, the angle of his own body, the look of the sidewalk. He did not experience the memory as something faded and distant; instead, it could arrive suddenly and with such force that he would feel as though the scene were happening again. At times, especially when he heard shouting in the school corridors or in the lunchroom, he would freeze for a moment, his body reacting before he could think, as if the threat had returned in the present. He was especially aware of his neck at those moments; a sharp or familiar ache there could pull him right back into the robbery with unsettling immediacy. Even in safe settings, such as his apartment in the evenings or the staff room at school, he found that he could not fully settle. He described himself as unable to relax even when he knew he was in a safe place, because some part of him remained on alert, waiting for another sudden confrontation.

That alertness became visible in the way he moved through daily life. Daniel began scanning exits as soon as he entered any room or building, a habit he noticed in classrooms, grocery stores, and even when he visited a friend’s apartment. At school, where he worked with children who sometimes shouted in frustration or excitement, he found himself orienting to doors and windows before he had even put down his bag. The building felt less like a workplace and more like a place to map for escape routes. He also became wary around police after the robbery, and any unexpected sight of an officer outside the school or near his neighborhood could make him tense and watchful, as if official attention signaled that something bad might still be unfolding. Daniel understood these reactions as a sign that he had to be on guard all the time. He had come to believe that someone else would not have gotten into this situation, that another man would have seen it coming, handled it better, or somehow avoided it altogether. That comparison sat heavily with him and fed a growing sense that he was inadequate, not only for having been robbed but for the way the experience still seemed to linger in him.

The emotional meaning he attached to the memory was also complicated. When he remembered the robbery, he felt intense rage, especially at the men who had cornered him and at the unfairness of being targeted while simply walking home from work. Alongside that anger, however, he also felt guilt. He replayed the incident repeatedly and judged himself for not having done more to protect himself, as though there had been a better version of the event in which he could have prevented it. This mixture of rage and guilt made the memory hard to sit with, so he began trying to push it away, though it could still intrude when he least expected it. Over time, these experiences affected how he moved through his days and how fully he could inhabit his teaching role. He kept working, but the effort of staying vigilant, watching exits, and bracing for shouting left him worn down. By the time he sought help, Daniel was tired of living as if he were still under threat, and he wanted to understand why his body and mind remained on alert long after the robbery had ended. What he feared most was that he would never fully feel safe again; what he hoped for was a way to walk into a room, hear a raised voice, or see a police car without immediately feeling himself pulled back to that street.
